post_title: European stagnation is real
text: Rebutting Krugman, the post argues that the EU-US gap is real and understated by current-price PPP comparisons: at constant prices US output has pulled away since 2000, the gains are not just a tech accounting artefact, and they are not explained by inequality or hours worked. The divergence is presented as 'the strongest evidence for reform in Europe'.

post_title: European stagnation is real
text: Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon are together worth more than all European stock markets combined.
original_source: Authors' figure; European market value from FESE Annual Statistical Report 2025 (https://www.fese.eu/app/uploads/2024/08/fese-annual-statistical-report-2025.pdf)

post_title: European stagnation is real
text: Share of US equity held by American households and institutions; European households (outside the Netherlands, Switzerland, Nordics) hold little equity, so they capture less of US tech profits.

post_title: European stagnation is real
text: Median equivalised disposable household income (after taxes and transfers, PPP-adjusted): the median American earns 30% more than the median Dutch person, about 31% more than the median German and about 52% more than the median French person (2021 data).
original_source: OECD Society at a Glance 2024 (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/society-at-a-glance-2024_918d8db3-en/full-report/household-income_3ee61044.html); Luxembourg Income Study chart shows a similar, slightly smaller gap

post_title: European stagnation is real
text: Labour productivity per hour grew 6.7% in the US from Q4 2019 to Q2 2024, against 0.9% in Europe.
verified: original source differs: the ECB figure of 0.9% is for the euro area, not the EU as the post says; the 6.7% US figure and the period match

post_title: European stagnation is real
text: About half of the US-Europe gap in hours worked per person that existed in the 1990s had closed by the end of the 2010s, so hours cannot explain the post-2000 divergence in GDP.
original_source: Birinci, Karabarbounis and See, NBER Working Paper 35020 (2026) (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35020)

post_title: European stagnation is real
text: Entry-level pay comparisons: London police officer $57,000 vs Washington DC $75,000; Deloitte junior consultant in Madrid about €28,000 (~$33,000) vs $63,000 in Charlotte, NC.

post_title: European stagnation is real
text: Tech margins stay well above marginal cost (Apple margins about 40%, Anthropic inference margins 70%), so much of the productivity gain from tech stays as US profit rather than passing to European consumers.
original_source: Apple: authors' figure; Anthropic: post on X by RHouseResearch (https://x.com/RHouseResearch/status/2050607601830768795)

post_title: European stagnation is real
text: Agglomeration (Krugman 1991) means tech leadership reinforces itself. Europe is not just buying the same iPhones; it is being pushed out of the next round of tech industries, which will cluster where existing ones already are.

post_title: The Mismeasurement of European Productivity (Revised)
text: Aghion, Bergeaud and Garicano argue that a chain of current-PPP comparisons cannot measure real growth because it changes the price yardstick every year. National-deflator series all show US productivity growing about a point a year faster than France's for three decades, so Europe's productivity gap is 'not an accounting issue'.

post_title: The Mismeasurement of European Productivity (Revised)
text: By 2024 the actual France-US PPP and the PPP implied by carrying the 1995 value forward with national deflators are about 18 log points apart, enough to cancel nearly all of the measured France-US growth divergence.
original_source: Authors' calculation from OECD data; technical note by Bergeaud (https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/slyz92wyez8sycja0qnvq/PPP.pdf); consistent with Inklaar (2026) draft research note

post_title: The Mismeasurement of European Productivity (Revised)
text: Information technology is about 8% of US private-sector output but produced about 45% of US productivity growth since 1988.
original_source: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, Chicago Fed Letter 2025 no. 515 (https://www.chicagofed.org/publications/chicago-fed-letter/2025/515)
verified: original source checked (the 45% refers to total factor productivity growth; the 8% is IT's average share of private business output)

post_title: The Mismeasurement of European Productivity (Revised)
text: Annual real labour productivity growth (national deflators): US 1.93% vs France 0.85%. Converting GDP each year at current PPPs gives near-identical nominal rates (US 3.89, France 3.75), which hides the real gap.
original_source: Authors' table compiling seven productivity datasets (mostly national accounts)

post_title: The Mismeasurement of European Productivity (Revised)
text: The cumulative divergence is roughly one point of annual productivity growth for three decades, close to 18 log points by 2024. No proposed quality adjustment comes close to closing it.

post_title: The Mismeasurement of European Productivity (Revised)
text: The Eurostat-OECD PPP programme prices a shared list of about 2,500 consumer goods and services; the International Comparison Program splits GDP into about 155 basic headings.
original_source: Eurostat-OECD PPP programme / International Comparison Program, as described by the authors

post_title: The Mismeasurement of European Productivity (Revised)
text: Europe's real weaknesses are policy choices that can be changed: fragmented markets, firms that stay too small, shallow capital markets, slow diffusion of digital tools and too few tech companies built to global scale.

post_title: The two Europes
text: With Olivier Kooi, the post argues the EU is 'two economies that move in opposite directions'. Central and Eastern Europe is converging on the US while the rich West and South are falling behind. The Russian security shock is driving reform on the eastern frontier but not in the countries that need the Draghi agenda most.

post_title: The two Europes
text: GDP per capita as a share of the US level, 2000 to 2030 (IMF projection): Poland 34% to 67%, Romania 27% to 60%, Lithuania 29% to 69%, Bulgaria 23% to 53%.

post_title: The two Europes
text: GDP per capita as a share of the US level, 2000 to 2030: Portugal 64% to 57%, Spain 72% to 61%, France 86% to 71%, Italy 93% to 68%.

post_title: The two Europes
text: Each 750 km (one standard deviation) closer to Moscow predicts about 0.30 pp of GDP more defence spending after 2022 (s.e. 0.09) and 0.39 pp more public investment (s.e. 0.12). Defence, education and investment combined move by about 0.9 pp.

post_title: The two Europes
text: Each additional 1,000 km from Moscow correlates with about 1.07 pp of GDP higher pension spending in 2022 and 0.49 pp more projected growth in pension spending by 2040.
original_source: Authors' calculations from European Commission 2024 Ageing Report

post_title: What Draghi gets wrong
text: EU competition enforcement is one of the things the EU has got right. Draghi's and Ribera's push to loosen merger and state-aid rules for scale risks crony capitalism and a more fragmented single market. Regulatory fragmentation, not antitrust, is what blocks cross-border mergers, and the EU should simplify regulation while keeping antitrust strong.

post_title: What Draghi gets wrong
text: Mergers among US listed firms led to a 30% increase in lobbying spending, linking market power to political power.
original_source: Cowgill, Prat and Valletti (2021), 'Political power and market power', arXiv:2106.13612

post_title: What Draghi gets wrong
text: Monthly mobile prices are around €15 in Europe against €43 in the US, which the post credits to EU merger control blocking 4-to-3 consolidations.

post_title: What Draghi gets wrong
text: The UK CMA let Vodafone-Three merge, creating an operator with 27 million customers.

post_title: Failure Costs
text: Following Coste and Coatanlem, the post argues that Europe lacks disruptive innovation and a trillion-dollar firm because failure is too expensive: employment-protection rules make restructuring about ten times costlier than in the US. That lowers the expected value of risky bets, and VC returns, in high-failure sectors.

post_title: Failure Costs
text: Restructuring costs are about ten times higher in Western Europe than in the US.
original_source: Coatanlem and Coste (2024), 'Cost of Failure and Competitiveness in Disruptive Innovation', IEP@BU Policy Brief (https://iep.unibocconi.eu/sites/default/files/media/attach/PB24_%20Coatanlem%2C%20Coste%20%281%29.pdf)

post_title: Failure Costs
text: A significant restructuring at a large firm costs the equivalent of 2-4 months of pay per worker in the US, around 24 months in France and 30 months in Germany.
original_source: Coste estimate; chart attributed to Bloomberg (April 2023)
verified: original source differs: the Coatanlem-Coste brief uses 4 months of pay (US) vs 2 years (Europe) as a conservative illustration; the France 24 / Germany 30 month figures do not appear in its text (the post attributes them to a Bloomberg chart)

post_title: Failure Costs
text: Higher European restructuring costs imply an ex-ante VC internal rate of return about 4 points lower. The observed EU-US gap in VC IRR is about 5 points.

post_title: Failure Costs
text: Worked example: a project with a 1-in-5 success chance, $100m payoff and $15m cost has expected value +$4.2m in California ($1m restructuring cost) but -$3m in Germany ($10m restructuring cost).

post_title: Failure Costs
text: Between 2014 and 2019, average returns on invested capital at large companies were 20% lower in the EU than in the US, with 90% of the difference due to ICT and pharmaceuticals.
original_source: McKinsey Global Institute (2022), 'Securing Europe's competitiveness: Addressing its technology gap'

post_title: Failure Costs
text: Moving to US-style employment protection would raise R&D intensity by 54% in France, 33% in Germany, 32% in the Netherlands and 41% in Italy.
original_source: Cette, Lopez and Mairesse (2018), Economie et Statistique 503-504

post_title: Failure Costs
text: SAP's AI investment is about $0.6bn a year, two orders of magnitude below US peers (e.g. Google R&D $43bn in 2023, Meta $37bn on compute in 2024). For its 8,000 layoffs SAP provisions over 18 months of pay globally and more than three years in Europe.

post_title: Failure Costs
text: Atos spent 10% of revenue on restructuring in 2022.

post_title: Failure Costs
text: The Draghi report calls restructuring costs a source of 'huge disadvantage' but does not mention them again in 300+ pages. EPL is not an EU competence, and the OECD EPL index is a qualitative reading of statutes, so the scale of the problem is poorly measured.

post_title: It is all about the superstars
text: US leadership comes from a few superstar firms, and EU rules such as the new Product Liability Directive (software as a product, no-fault liability) and the AI Act 'compress the distribution' and deter the risky experimentation that produces superstars. Every policy should be tested by asking 'What does this do for my outliers?'

post_title: It is all about the superstars
text: The revised Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853 makes software a product under no-fault liability, with liability for defects up to 10 years after release. For AI, courts may presume defectiveness without proof of a causal link.

post_title: It is all about the superstars
text: Superstar concentration: 80% of space cargo is launched by SpaceX; up to 95% of AI chips are designed by one firm; the three frontier AI labs have about 8,000 employees combined, no more than 0.2% of the tech sector.

post_title: It is all about the superstars
text: Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Apple and Microsoft together spend almost twice as much on R&D as the entire EU public sector.

post_title: It is all about the superstars
text: The ≈7.5 million people of the Bay Area have created more tech value than the ≈750 million people of Europe.

post_title: It is all about the superstars
text: Israel raised $5.9bn in venture investment in 2022, three times Italy's total.

post_title: It is all about the superstars
text: Nokia announced up to 14,000 job cuts after a 21% sales drop, but labour rules in Germany, France and Finland mean the restructuring will not finish until 2026.
original_source: Coatanlem and Coste (2024), IEP@BU Policy Brief

post_title: It is all about the superstars
text: AIFMD rules for funds over $500 million restrict VC participation to accredited 'professional investors'. Solvency II treats VC as high-risk, limiting insurers' venture funding.
original_source: Arnold, Claveres and Frie (2024), IMF Working Paper 'Stepping Up Venture Capital to Finance Innovation in Europe'

post_title: Focus on the Micro, not the Macro
text: Europe's stagnation comes from microeconomic constraints, not too little public spending. During its supposedly 'neoliberal' period the EU kept adding rules on product liability, the environment and digital, and the cure is structural reform: a single market for services, simpler regulation and fewer environmental and digital rules, not debt-funded industrial policy.

post_title: Focus on the Micro, not the Macro
text: Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Cyprus, which carried out structural reforms during the euro crisis, outperformed the rest of the euro area in output and job creation over the past decade.
original_source: Filip, Masuch, Setzer and Valenta, ECB Blog, 3 Dec 2024 (https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/blog/date/2024/html/ecb.blog20241203~5d969f5a3b.en.html)

post_title: Focus on the Micro, not the Macro
text: National measures to shield consumers and firms from the energy crisis cost €651bn in the 16 months to January 2023.

post_title: Focus on the Micro, not the Macro
text: European labour productivity growth since 2015 has been stuck at 0.7% a year, which accounts for more than half of the per-capita GDP growth gap with the US. Draghi: 'around 70% of the gap in per capita GDP with the US at PPP is explained by lower productivity'.

post_title: Focus on the Micro, not the Macro
text: Italy's Superbonus covered 110% of home renovation costs. Budgeted at €35bn, it ballooned to about €225bn, over 10% of GDP and nearly triple Italy's RRF grants.
original_source: Boeri and Perotti (2023); Giavazzi and Goretti (2024)

post_title: Focus on the Micro, not the Macro
text: NextGenerationEU will need around €30bn a year in debt service from 2028. About 70% of the EU budget comes from GNI-based national contributions.

post_title: Focus on the Micro, not the Macro
text: Implicit pension liabilities are approaching 400% of GDP for France and Italy.

post_title: Focus on the Micro, not the Macro
text: Draghi's CEPR lecture: from 2009 to 2019 the euro area's cyclically adjusted fiscal stance averaged 0.3% against -3.9% in the US, and US primary deficits were 14 times larger (€7.8tn vs €560bn).

post_title: Why Sweden has so many unicorns
text: With Per Strömberg, the post argues Europe's VC gap is a demand problem, not a supply one: capital crosses borders, but there are too few investable start-ups. Sweden's unicorns come from an angel ecosystem of recycled exit proceeds, helped by a 2003 tax deferral, deep multi-tier equity markets and the abolition of wealth and inheritance taxes.

post_title: Why Sweden has so many unicorns
text: Sweden has 48 unicorns for 10 million people, the fourth most per capita in the world (after Israel, Iceland and the US) and the fourth most in Europe in absolute terms. Italy has one-third as many despite a GDP more than four times larger.

post_title: Why Sweden has so many unicorns
text: Europe's share of global venture capital rose from about 5% to 20% by 2022. 65 cities in 25 European countries had at least one unicorn as of July 2023.

post_title: Why Sweden has so many unicorns
text: 44% of VC invested in European companies comes from outside Europe. In 2016 Austria, Ireland, Sweden and Spain each got over 70% of VC from foreign investors.
original_source: Bradley, Duruflé, Hellmann and Wilson (2019), JRFM (https://www.econstor.eu/bitstream/10419/239042/1/1668837862.pdf), using Dealroom data

post_title: Why Sweden has so many unicorns
text: Swedish market capitalisation was 169% of GDP in 2023, more than double the EU27 average of 69%. Sweden recorded 823 IPOs between 2016 and 2023, the most in the EU, nearly 90% on SME growth markets.

post_title: Why Sweden has so many unicorns
text: The Swedish government's share of total VC investment fell from 25% on average in 2011-2013 to 6% in 2021.

post_title: Why Sweden has so many unicorns
text: Angel tax credits in 31 US states raised angel investment volume by about one-fifth but improved no real outcome (young-firm jobs, entry, patents, exits). Fewer than 1% of recipients were professional investors.
original_source: Denes, Howell, Mezzanotti, Wang and Xu (2023), Journal of Finance (https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/faculty/mezzanotti/documents/tax_credit_hm.pdf)

post_title: Why Sweden has so many unicorns
text: VC economics: management fee about 2%, carry about 20%, total fees 5-7% of invested capital. VC needs gross returns about 10 points above listed equity.

post_title: The Smart Second Mover, Part II
text: With Jesús Saa-Requejo, the post says the EU should seed a missing AI 'implementation layer'. Its tools would be public procurement on open, swappable interfaces with purchasing devolved to users (modelled on Ukraine's drone market), plus a European digital tax that large digital firms could pay by capitalising joint ventures with European partners (drawing on China's auto JV lessons). Open standards and interoperability rules are 'necessary' but 'not sufficient'.

post_title: The Smart Second Mover, Part II
text: Ukraine went from seven drone manufacturers before 2022 to over 500 by 2025, producing four million units a year and attracting over $100m a year in private investment.
original_source: Washington Post (https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2025/09/06/ukraine-drone-industry-export/); Kyiv Independent; Kyiv Post

post_title: The Smart Second Mover, Part II
text: Ukraine's Ministry of Defence allocated over $2.5bn to domestic drone makers in 2024-2025. 96% of state FPV drone purchases went to domestic producers, and Brave1 gave over 540 grants totalling $50m.

post_title: The Smart Second Mover, Part II
text: In China's auto joint ventures, domestic models had 65% more defects than JV models in 2001 but only 33% more by 2014, showing spillovers through workers and suppliers.
original_source: Bai, Barwick, Cao and Li (2025), AER, using J.D. Power IQS data (https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257%2Faer.20221501)

post_title: The Smart Second Mover, Part II
text: Public spending on defence, health, education and administration accounts for up to half of European GDP, yet barely touches AI.

post_title: Nineteen thoughts on AI and Europe
text: With Simon Grimm, the post argues Europe should accept dependence on American frontier AI and become a heavy user, as it did with US software, rather than build a 'sovereign' model or 'Buy European' worse models. National governments control the factors that matter (energy, permitting, labour markets, taxes) more than the Commission does.

post_title: Nineteen thoughts on AI and Europe
text: Meta will spend more on chips this year ($125bn) than Germany spends on defence ($114bn).

post_title: Nineteen thoughts on AI and Europe
text: Mistral's reported revenue earlier this year was less than 1% of Anthropic's today.
original_source: Epoch AI data on AI companies (https://epoch.ai/data/ai-companies)

post_title: Nineteen thoughts on AI and Europe
text: European data centres interviewed said Europe would not build data centres at scale without subsidies, citing high power prices. US firms also avoid large EU investments because of political risk: fear of changing copyright rules, fines and 'extractive taxes' once capital is committed.
original_source: Authors' interviews with European data centres

post_title: Nineteen thoughts on AI and Europe
text: Europe's 2005 Franco-German 'own Google' effort (Quaero, and Germany's Theseus spin-off) was discontinued by 2013.

post_title: The EU and the not-so-simple macroeconomics of AI
text: In an Epoch AI podcast, Garicano argues that the AI Act and GDPR make AI adoption in Europe 'costly and slow' just when growth is needed. Europe risks 'R without G': paying higher global interest rates from the AI investment boom without the productivity gains, made worse by demographics and high explicit and implicit debt.

post_title: The EU and the not-so-simple macroeconomics of AI
text: Garicano says about 15 papers on GDPR all find less venture capital investment, fewer start-ups and higher compliance costs.
original_source: Garicano's own summary (see Silicon Continent post 'Is GDPR undermining innovation in Europe')

post_title: The EU and the not-so-simple macroeconomics of AI
text: High-risk AI under the AI Act (including education and health) requires error-free, unbiased training data, detailed logs, documentation kept for ten years, conformity assessment and registration. There are 55 EU authorities involved.
original_source: Garicano's description of the EU AI Act

post_title: The EU and the not-so-simple macroeconomics of AI
text: Europe has about two foundation models against about 15 in the US.

post_title: The EU and the not-so-simple macroeconomics of AI
text: The AI Act's systemic-risk threshold for general-purpose AI is 10^25 training FLOP. GPT-4 and Llama are already above it.
original_source: EU AI Act (as discussed in the interview)

post_title: The EU and the not-so-simple macroeconomics of AI
text: France's explicit public debt is almost 120% of GDP, with implicit pension debt of 3-4 times GDP.

post_title: The EU and the not-so-simple macroeconomics of AI
text: Juniors in AI-exposed occupations: a study of about 62 million workers finds junior employment falling through less hiring while senior employment grows. 'Canaries in the Coal Mine' finds drops for workers aged 22-25.
original_source: Lichtinger and Hosseini Maasoum (2025), SSRN (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5425555); Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen (2025) (https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/publications/canaries-in-the-coal-mine/)

post_title: The EU and the not-so-simple macroeconomics of AI
text: Global asset demand has multiplied by four over the past 40 years, pushing rates down. AI is expected to reverse this and raise interest rates.
original_source: Auclert, Malmberg, Rognlie and Straub (2025), 'The Race Between Asset Supply and Asset Demand' (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5757603)

post_title: The EU and the not-so-simple macroeconomics of AI
text: Data-centre build-out runs to hundreds of billions a year, up to a trillion by 2030, far beyond any public budget. The EU's AI gigafactories plan covers five large AI data centres.

post_title: The EU and the not-so-simple macroeconomics of AI
text: EU error correction is weak: the same Commission, Parliament and Council coalition that passed the 2019-2024 wave of Green Deal and digital legislation is now asked to undo it. Garicano notes Parliament initially rejected even the first omnibus on corporate reporting.

post_title: The Problem Isn't Public R&D
text: Europe's innovation gap is not a shortfall in public R&D, where it spends as much as the US relative to GDP. The gap is private: R&D concentrated in US tech firms, sector composition and thin venture capital. EU flagships such as the Human Brain Project show public money poorly spent.

post_title: The Problem Isn't Public R&D
text: Public-sector R&D is about 0.74% of GDP in Europe against 0.69% in the US (2021 government R&D roughly €108bn in the EU vs 131bn in the US).

post_title: The Problem Isn't Public R&D
text: Private-sector R&D is 1.3% of GDP in the EU against 2.4% in the US, a gap worth €341bn in 2021. More than half of that gap is attributable to the top 10 US tech firms.

post_title: The Problem Isn't Public R&D
text: Sector composition explains about 60% of the R&D gap. With a US-like structure, EU private R&D would be 2.2% of GDP.
original_source: Fuest, Gros, Mengel, Presidente and Tirole (2024), 'EU Innovation Policy: How to Escape the Middle Technology Trap'

post_title: The Problem Isn't Public R&D
text: The top 5 US tech firms (Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Apple, Microsoft) spent about $202bn on R&D in 2022.

post_title: The Problem Isn't Public R&D
text: Venture capital is 0.05% of GDP in Europe against 0.32% in the US. US seed-to-late-stage VC is no more than $170bn a year.
original_source: Arnold, Claveres and Frie (2024), IMF Working Paper (cited in references)

post_title: The Problem Isn't Public R&D
text: Horizon 2020 was funded at €77bn and Horizon Europe (2021-27) at €95.5bn. 70% of high-quality Horizon proposals go unfunded. The EIC Pathfinder had €250m for 2024, against DARPA $4.1bn, ARPA-H $1.5bn and ARPA-E $0.5bn.
original_source: EU Publications Office (https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/cd9586b5-db2d-11e8-afb3-01aa75ed71a1/language-en); eufunds.me; Draghi report

post_title: The Problem Isn't Public R&D
text: US Defense Department R&D is less than 10% of total US R&D.

post_title: The Problem Isn't Public R&D
text: The Human Brain Project got €600m from 2013 to 2020 and is widely seen as a failure. DeepMind, funded by US investors, was bought by Google for 400m in 2014.

post_title: What explains heterogeneity in AI adoption?
text: A US-Europe AI adoption gap is opening, much like the ICT gap, and the gap within Europe (UK, Sweden and the Netherlands ahead of Germany, France and Italy) is as striking. Much of what composition does not explain traces to management practices, which 'will be much harder to solve than repealing the AI Act or GDPR'.

post_title: What explains heterogeneity in AI adoption?
text: Output per hour rose 85% in the US but 29% in the eurozone between 1995 and 2025.
original_source: Bick et al. (2026), Figure 1 (BLS and ECB data)

post_title: What explains heterogeneity in AI adoption?
text: In early 2026, 43% of US workers used generative AI at work against 32% on average in six European countries (UK 36%, France 28%, Italy 26%). AI accounted for 5.2% of US work hours, about double Northern Europe and triple Germany, France and Italy.
original_source: Bick, Blandin, Deming, Fuchs-Schündeln and Jessen (2026), 'Mind the Gap: AI Adoption in Europe and the U.S.', Brookings Papers / NBER WP 34995 (https://www.brookings.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/6_Bick-et-al_unembargoed.pdf)

post_title: What explains heterogeneity in AI adoption?
text: 7% of US firms use AI to produce goods or services against 4% of EU firms.
original_source: Bick et al. (2026), using the US BTOS and the EU ICT usage survey

post_title: What explains heterogeneity in AI adoption?
text: Demographics, occupation, industry and firm size explain 55% of the average US-Europe adoption gap (10.9 pp on average); the rest is unexplained.

post_title: What explains heterogeneity in AI adoption?
text: Management scores correlate with AI adoption across countries (0.81). In the UK, 2% of bottom-decile-managed firms adopt AI against 20% in the top decile. One SD on a personnel-management index is linked to 9.6 pp more adoption.
original_source: Bick et al. (2026), using World Management Survey data

post_title: What explains heterogeneity in AI adoption?
text: US police departments that adopted IT together with CompStat-style reorganisation raised clearance rates by 3.2 pp; those that bought IT without reorganising gained nothing.
original_source: Garicano and Heaton (2010), Journal of Labor Economics (https://www.rand.org/content/dam/rand/pubs/reprints/2010/RAND_RP1409.pdf)
